title: Power, product, and quotient rules
note: Power rule: d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹ for any real n, so rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first. The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives: (fg)′ = f′g + fg′, and (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g².

read.title: Why the product rule has two terms
text: It is tempting to guess that the derivative of f times g is f′ times g′. A quick test shows otherwise: x · x = x² has derivative 2x, but the derivatives of x and x multiply to 1.

Picture a rectangle whose width is f and whose height is g, so its area is fg. Let x change by a small amount. The width grows by about f′ times that change, and the height by about g′ times it. The new area adds two thin strips: one along the height, of size f′g, and one along the width, of size fg′. There is also a tiny corner piece, but it is a product of two small changes and vanishes in the limit. What remains is (fg)′ = f′g + fg′.

The quotient rule follows from the product rule and the chain rule, and the order of its numerator matters: (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g². A common memory aid is "low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared." When a quotient is easy to split, as in (2x + 3)/x = 2 + 3/x, rewriting first with the power rule is often faster and less error-prone.
